rows.gloss: day-group joined-with sun-etc-three or Friday or another

items.question: What counts as a yoga-occasion and when may it be observed?
premises: A day-group joined with the sun and the next two, or with Friday, or with another such factor is called a yoga-occasion.
This yoga-occasion is well known in the tradition.
It may be observed either at night or by day.
items.inference: A yoga-occasion is defined by specific calendrical conjunctions and is valid for observance in either part of the day.
uncertainties: The exact calendrical meaning of arkāditraya (sun and the next two) is compressed and may refer to a specific weekday or planetary sequence.
items.plain_english: A day joined with the sun and the two that follow, or with Friday, or with another such conjunction, is known as a yoga-occasion. It may be observed either at night or during the day.

items.question: What worship should be performed on yoga-occasions?
premises: Body-worship should certainly be performed on a yoga-occasion.
A wise person should honor all days called yoga-occasions.
This honoring is done through body-worship.
items.inference: The prescribed observance for every yoga-occasion is body-worship performed by the wise practitioner.
uncertainties: The exact ritual content of mūrtiyāga (body-worship) is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: On a yoga-occasion, body-worship should be performed in every way. A wise person should honor all days known as yoga-occasions through this worship.

items.question: What status can body-worship confer and where is this taught?
premises: Through body-worship a person can become a vow-holder.
This can occur even without a mandala.
This teaching about body-worship is given in the Siddhayogishvari tradition.
items.inference: Body-worship alone is sufficient to establish vow-holder status, according to the Siddhayogishvari teaching.
uncertainties: The precise ritual or initiatory threshold implied by samayī is not fully spelled out here.
items.plain_english: By performing body-worship, even without a mandala, a person can become a vow-holder. This is the teaching on body-worship found in the revered Siddhayogishvari tradition.

rows.gloss: in the Ratnamala and Trishiras scriptures

items.question: Which sources present the thread-offering rite spoken by Shiva?
premises: The thread-offering rite spoken by Shiva is now being presented.
It is set forth clearly.
It is also indicated in the Ratnamala and Trishiras scriptures.
items.inference: The thread-offering rite has a clear Shiva-given form and is further attested in two named scriptural recensions.
uncertainties: The verse distinguishes a clear exposition from indications in two scriptures, but does not specify how the recensions differ.
items.plain_english: Now the thread-offering rite spoken by Shiva is presented clearly. It is also indicated again in the revered Ratnamala and Trishiras scriptures.

rows.gloss: in the Siddha, Atana, Sadbhava, Malini, and Sara teachings

items.question: Which recension is given priority for the thread-offering rite?
premises: The rite appears in the Siddha, Atana, Sadbhava, Malini, and Sara teachings.
Among these, the form stated in the revered Mala is given priority.
That principal form of the rite is now being spoken.
items.inference: The exposition will follow the Mala recension as the primary authority among several scriptural sources.
uncertainties: The exact scope of each named teaching in the compound is compressed and may reflect a traditional list rather than a single text.
items.plain_english: Among the Siddha, Atana, Sadbhava, Malini, and Sara teachings, the rite is spoken here principally as stated in the revered Mala.

rows.gloss: fainted by sleep from poison born of churning the milk-ocean

items.question: Why could the serpent-king not remain in his own world during the cloud season?
premises: The serpent-king had fainted into a sleep caused by poison born from the churning of the milk-ocean.
This condition affected him during the cloud season.
Because of this, he did not dwell in his own world.
items.inference: The serpent-king's affliction made his own realm uninhabitable for him in the rainy season.
uncertainties: The verse implies but does not explicitly state the causal link between the poison-sleep and leaving his world.
items.plain_english: The serpent-king, overcome by a sleep brought on by the poison born from the churning of the milk-ocean, did not remain in his own world during the cloud season.

items.question: How did the serpent-king worship Bhairava during his exile?
premises: The serpent-king remained pure and lived on wind alone.
He continued this discipline for a hundred divine years, described as tenfold.
During that time he fully worshipped Lord Bhairava.
items.inference: The serpent-king responded to his affliction with prolonged ascetic worship of Bhairava.
uncertainties: The phrase divyaṃ daśaguṇaṃ is metrically and semantically compressed; its exact numerical force is unclear.
items.plain_english: Remaining pure and living only on wind, he fully worshipped Lord Bhairava for a hundred divine years, tenfold in measure.

items.question: What request did the serpent-king make to the pleased Bhairava?
premises: After long worship, the serpent-king addressed the pleased lord.
He said he was unable to stay in his own netherworld during the rains.
The supreme lord then responded to him.
items.inference: The serpent-king sought refuge from the supreme lord because he could not endure the rainy season in his own realm.
uncertainties: The verse ends mid-response, so the lord's action is completed only in the next verse.
items.plain_english: He then appealed to the pleased lord, saying that he was unable to remain in his own netherworld during the rains. The supreme lord responded to him.

rows.gloss: placed on the seat of his own matted-hair mass
he was held by all hosts of gods

items.question: How did the supreme lord provide refuge for the serpent-king?
premises: The supreme lord placed the serpent on the seat of his own matted-hair mass.
After that, all hosts of gods held the serpent on their own heads.
The serpent thus received a place of honor and refuge.
items.inference: The serpent-king was elevated from exile to a position of universal honor through the lord's protection.
uncertainties: The shift from singular refuge on Shiva's head to being held by all gods is compressed and may be symbolic.
items.plain_english: The supreme lord placed the serpent on the seat of his own matted hair. Then all the hosts of gods bore him upon their own heads.

rows.gloss: therefore on the head of the great lord

items.question: What does the serpent's elevation show about honor among the great?
premises: For those who are great and honored, worldwide honor is not surprising.
The serpent was placed on the head of the great lord.
He was also honored by the gods in every way.
items.inference: The serpent's universal honor follows naturally from being received by the great lord and the gods.
uncertainties: The verse functions as a general maxim; its exact syntactic completion carries into the next verse.
items.plain_english: For the great and honored, worldwide reverence is no wonder. Therefore, being placed on the head of the great lord and honored by all the gods is fitting.

rows.grounds: refers to the honored serpent-thread symbol

rows.gloss: one should make preceded by worship

items.question: How should one make the sacred thread and how great is its merit?
premises: One should make that sacred thread for oneself preceded by worship.
The thread-offering is being praised as supremely meritorious.
Even ten crores of ordinary worships are not equal to it.
items.inference: The thread-offering, properly made with worship, surpasses vast amounts of ordinary worship.
uncertainties: The referent of taṃ (that thread/that serpent) is contextually clear but syntactically compressed.
items.plain_english: One should make that sacred thread for oneself, preceded by worship. In the thread-offering, even ten crores of ordinary acts of worship are not equal to it.

rows.gloss: without the thread and so on this the serpent would take away

items.question: Why is the thread-offering indispensable even alongside initiation and knowledge?
premises: Without the thread-offering and related rites, initiation is in vain.
Without it, knowledge and even guru-worship are in vain.
By Shiva's command, the serpent would take away that merit if the thread-offering is omitted.
items.inference: The thread-offering is required to secure the fruits of initiation, knowledge, and guru-worship.
uncertainties: The object of haret (what exactly is taken away) is implied as the merit or efficacy of those acts rather than stated explicitly.
items.plain_english: Without the thread-offering and the rites that go with it, initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and even worship of the guru is in vain. By Shiva's command, the serpent would take that away.
